title: I killed 20 of my own trading hypotheses. Here's the bug that fooled me first.
author: Foreign-Safe-8161

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The fee decomposition is the part more people should copy. Splitting P&L into price movement versus cost turns "tune the stops" into "is there signal at all", and those are completely different projects.

On the t-stat: with a 168 bar horizon your effective sample is closer to 9311/168, about 55, not 9311. Deflating by sqrt(168) puts 16.9 at roughly 1.3, which lands under the bar instead of miles over it. Newey-West with a 168 lag gets there more carefully, but the back of the envelope already tells the story.

Did any of the 20 survive once you corrected for the overlap?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Almost none.  
After properly correcting for overlapping windows (and multiple testing), the picture became much cleaner and uglier:  
•  The vast majority were simply noise. Several that looked decent before the overlap correction collapsed to t-stats well under 1.  
•  A few were reclassified from “rejected” to “untestable” — the measurement itself was blind at those horizons/costs, so a zero result didn’t actually tell us anything useful.  
•  One known academic result survived cleanly (volatility risk premium on S&P 500, t ≈ 8), but it’s not implementable from a retail account.  
•  One hypothesis is still open (open interest + basis divergence). The sign is consistent across instruments and horizons, but we don’t have enough independent observations yet to say whether it’s tradable. Data is still being collected.  
So out of the original 20, effectively zero new tradable edges survived the full set of corrections. The overlap adjustment was one of the more painful ones — it turned a couple of “promising” results into obvious noise.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Zero out of 20 is a result, not a failure. The bucket worth keeping is the untestable one. Most people only carry works and doesn't work, and a horizon where the measurement is blind looks identical to a dead hypothesis in that scheme.

Is the open interest one on a fixed sample target, or do you stop when the sign flips?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Fixed sample target.  
I calculated the number of independent observations needed on each horizon so the detection threshold falls below costs (power 0.80). For the 3-hour horizon that’s roughly 43 days. The collector is just running until that point.  
I’m deliberately not stopping on sign flips or early t-stats — that would defeat the purpose of pre-registering the test.  
I’m still looking, mostly in directions that aren’t pure price data. If you have ideas that survive the kind of scrutiny above, I’m happy to hear them.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Pre-registering the stop is the part almost nobody does, and it's the whole difference between a test and a search.

One thing worth writing down now is what you'll do if it lands just short of threshold at day 43. That's the moment the temptation to extend shows up. Have you decided that in advance?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Yes. If it’s short of the threshold at the pre-registered sample size, the test fails.  
I don’t get to extend. That would turn the pre-registration into theatre. The only planned continuation is the second, event-based version of the same idea (already written down), and only if the continuous version is flatly negative — not if it’s “almost”.  
Borderline results get treated as negative. The temptation to keep going is exactly why the stop has to be decided in advance.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Refusing to extend is the whole game. Extending is where most people quietly convert a null into a positive.

Do you write the event-based version down before you see the continuous result, or after? Writing it first is the only thing stopping it becoming a second bite at the same data.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Before. Always before.  
If I wrote the event-based specification after seeing the continuous results, the continuous test would just be an exploratory EDA step disguised as a benchmark. That defeats the entire purpose of a pre-registration hash.  
Both versions (the continuous ⁠oi\_price\_div⁠ and the event-driven 95th percentile trigger) live inside the exact same pre-registered spec file with the same commit hash. The branching logic is strict:  
1. Run Continuous Spec \\to Evaluated at target sample size.  
2. If Continuous meets criteria \\to Validated (Proceed to forward tracking).  
3. If Continuous fails flatly \\to Proceed to Event-Based Spec.  
4. If Continuous is "borderline" \\to Hard fail. The entire line of inquiry dies. Event-based branch is discarded without execution.  
Writing the triggers, execution rules, and stop criteria before touching the data is the only reason the secondary hypothesis retains any statistical validity.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Two variants in one spec file is still two tests, and that's the part I'd want pinned down. If the event version only gets run when the continuous one fails, that second look costs you something.

Does your threshold account for that, or is each version judged at its own alpha?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Excellent point, and that's the exact distinction between naive sequential testing and adjusted alpha thresholds.  
Each version is **not** judged at an unadjusted standalone \\alpha. Running a secondary hypothesis unconditionally inflates the Family-Wise Error Rate (\\text{FWER}).  
To account for the "second look" penalty:  
1. **Alpha Penalty / Split:** The significance threshold for the secondary (event-based) test isn't a standard p < 0.05. It operates under a strict adjustment (Bonferroni / Holm-Bonferroni variant), effectively requiring a much higher Minimum Detectable Effect (MDE) to pass than the primary test.  
2. **Conditional Gate (The "Borderline" Elimination):** As noted, if the continuous test yields a marginal/borderline signal, the path ends. The secondary test is *only* triggered on a flat-null continuous result to prevent fishing in fuzzy regimes.  
3. **Multiple Testing Correction:** The statistical significance of any discovery on the secondary branch is evaluated against the total hypothesis budget (k=2) assigned to that dataset.  
If you don't pay the \\alpha-penalty on the second test, you're just doing sequential P-hacking with better documentation.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
k=2 is the budget inside one hypothesis, but all 20 ran on the same price history. The family that matters is the whole program, not each pair.

Do you carry a running count across the 20, or does the budget reset with each new idea?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
fair call, and that distinction gets to the root of global vs hypothesis-level error rates.  
the hypothesis budget resets per pre-registered feature, but only because the global FWER across the broader 20-idea research cycle is controlled through a hard family-level hurdle rate rather than continuous p-value inflation.  
instead of scaling alpha dynamic penalties to k=20 (which quickly renders any statistical test useless due to over-conservatism), the framework enforces a global minimum effect size filter. any feature that fails to cover the combined friction baseline of 16 bps in the primary vectorized pass is killed instantly.  
so while k=2 handles internal sequential branching for a single registered feature, the overall 20-hypothesis search space is bounded by that upfront global MDE gate. if a feature can't clear the structural cost barrier outright, it doesn't get to consume any portion of the research alpha budget.  
И

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
A family level hurdle is a cleaner instrument than a per test alpha here, since it survives you adding idea 21 without renegotiating everything behind it.

The part I would want written down is what counts as one family. Is it the 20 idea cycle, or the feature, when one feature spawns two specs?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
A “family" is defined at the research cycle level (the 20-idea batch), not the individual feature level.  
if a single feature spawns two different specs (like varying lookbacks or execution thresholds), both specs consume budget within that same 20-idea batch. that stops hidden parameter sweeps from dodging FWER controls.  
the 16 bps MDE gate acts as the hard filter first. if a spec can't clear that friction barrier on the initial vectorized pass, it gets killed instantly without consuming an active alpha slot. that keeps the search space bounded and avoids over-conservative penalties.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
A screen run on the same sample is still a look at it. The specs the 16 bps gate kills don't stop being tests, they just leave the denominator, so the count you penalise ends up smaller than the number of times you queried the data.

Doesn't break the design. The family is just bigger than the surviving slots make it look.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
valid statistical nuance, but there's a distinction between hypothesis testing and structural feasibility.  
the 16 bps gate isn't an alpha test evaluating p-values—it's a hard friction barrier (spread + execution fees). a spec yielding 4 bps isn't rejected for lack of statistical significance; it's rejected because it physically cannot survive the exchange fee schedule.  
treating zero-margin structural noise as a candidate hypothesis inflates the denominator with dead specs that were never economically viable to begin with. total data queries are tracked for auditing, but penalizing statistical tests against physically impossible execution boundaries turns FWER controls overly conservative.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: The gate is deterministic, but the number feeding it is not. Spread is a distribution, so 16 bps is an estimate with variance around it, and a spec clearing at 18 bps can still be infeasible in the hours that actually matter. Do you set the gate off median spread or off a worse percentile?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
it's calculated off a stress-tested percentile (P75/P90 of realized spread + adverse selection during target volatility regimes), never the median.  
median spread is a trap for execution modeling. if a signal clears at 18 bps during quiet hours but the alpha only triggers during liquidity drains when spread blows out to 30 bps, the trade dies in real time.  
the 16 bps baseline scales dynamically with volatility-adjusted execution costs so specs aren't evaluated against unrealistically tight quotes.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
It depends which number the gate reads. If it compares the spec's measured edge against 16 bps, that's selection on the same statistic the t-test uses, since both share a numerator. If it compares a structural spread estimate that never touches the outcome, it's genuinely free.

Which of the two is it?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
it's the second one.  
the gate evaluates exogenous order book state (realized bid-ask spread and depth at time of trigger) independently of the strategy's expected return.  
if current book structure implies execution friction exceeds 16 bps at trigger time, the signal is dropped before measuring outcome or edge. evaluating edge against the threshold would indeed double-count the numerator, so keeping the market friction gate exogenous is mandatory to keep the statistical pass clean.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
That settles it. Dropping the signal before you measure outcome keeps the gate out of the inference entirely, so those specs never entered the family and your denominator is right as it stands.

I was arguing against the version where the threshold reads the edge. That isn't what you built.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body: Thx

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Anytime. That back and forth actually made me tighten how I define a family on my end, so it was useful both ways.

Are you fixing the idea budget per cycle, or letting it flex when a batch looks unusually good?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
it's strictly fixed per cycle.  
flexing the budget mid-stream based on early batch performance introduces dynamic selection bias—you end up expanding the family size N conditional on seeing favorable noise, which distorts the expected maximum Sharpe distribution under the null.  
if a batch looks unusually good, those trials still count against the pre-committed budget for that family, and any follow-up exploration goes into a fresh, separately penalized family container.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Pre-committing N is what makes the max-Sharpe correction mean anything, and flexing it mid-cycle turns 20 trials into an unbounded search. The cost is queueing though: an idea that arrives in week two either waits for the next cycle or inflates the family you already fixed. Do you hold those in a backlog, or does arrival order decide?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
they just go straight to a static backlog until the current cycle wraps up and the budget resets.  
if you let arrival order decide, you risk a subtle data-leakage bias—ideas generated mid-cycle are almost always subconsciously influenced by what the market's doing right now or how the early batch performed.  
queuing them keeps hypothesis generation truly orthogonal. once the active family is closed and penalized through DSR, we pull from the backlog based on core structural rationale rather than recent market behavior, then lock it into the next family with its own pre-committed N.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Logging when each idea was written, not just when it was tested, is what makes that leakage checkable later. You can go back and see whether mid-cycle ideas actually underperformed the ones written before the cycle opened.

Do you keep that write timestamp?

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body: yeah, write-timestamping is standard in the audit log. comparing pre-cycle vs mid-cycle generation performance down the line is actually a clean way to quantify lookahead and recency bias in the pipeline.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Worth remembering that split isn't randomised. Mid cycle ideas are conditioned on what the early results already showed you, so a gap between the two groups could be that conditioning rather than leakage. Still the right thing to log.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body: Got it 👏
